purpose: Methodological evidence cards for audience selection; not evidence of product demand.

cards.title: Methods of bank-client segmentation for transfers
cards.methodological_claim: The source summary describes comparing K-Means, DBSCAN, Mean Shift and hierarchical clustering with Dynamic Time Warping, and evaluating an ensemble by runtime, memory and silhouette score.
cards.limitations: This is a university thesis summary; the underlying bank data and full analysis are not part of the local corpus.
cards.transferability_note: Useful for evaluation design only; it does not establish demand for a current product or segment.

cards.title: Customer segmentation with Open Banking data
cards.methodological_claim: The abstract reports comparing RFM-based K-Means and DBSCAN on three months of anonymized UK Open Banking transactions; it frames cluster labels as behavioral/value groups and compares silhouette coefficients.
cards.limitations: Only the abstract is available; the study population, feature construction and validation details are incomplete.
cards.transferability_note: The UK banking sample and study-specific clusters cannot be treated as evidence about this dataset or Tempo demand.

cards.title: Interpretable customer segmentation in financial services
cards.methodological_claim: The source is focused on interpretable segmentation in financial services; it is relevant for requiring segment explanations that map to observable features rather than opaque persona narratives.
cards.limitations: The source context is financial services and its empirical setting does not match this synthetic exploratory segment set or a café scheduling product.
cards.transferability_note: Transfer the interpretability principle, not the source population, thresholds or commercial conclusions.

cards.title: Sequences of purchases in credit card data reveal lifestyles in urban populations
cards.methodological_claim: The paper studies purchase sequences as a way to characterize behavioral patterns. Observable transaction sequences can support behavioral profiling, but they do not directly observe motivations, needs or purchase intent.
cards.limitations: The data is a separate urban credit-card population and the paper explicitly describes data-access constraints.
cards.transferability_note: Use only the distinction between observed behavior and unobserved lifestyle or motivation; do not transfer lifestyle labels.

cards.title: Temporal fluidity in credit-card personas
cards.methodological_claim: The source concerns temporal fluidity of behavioral personas, supporting a check that segment assignments and feature profiles are not assumed to be stable merely because one snapshot clusters cleanly.
cards.limitations: The source population, observation window and persona construction differ from the current segment set.
cards.transferability_note: It supports asking for a temporal stability test; it does not show that the current segments are stable.

cards.title: Dynamic LRFMS and time-series clustering
cards.methodological_claim: The source uses dynamic LRFMS and time-series clustering, making it relevant to testing whether recency, frequency, monetary or related behavioral profiles change over time.
cards.limitations: The application domain is auto parts and its data-generating process is not the current synthetic banking dataset.
cards.transferability_note: Transfer the need to define observation windows and monitor change, not the segment meanings or outcomes.

cards.title: Longitudinal supermarket segmentation validation
cards.methodological_claim: The source is directly relevant to longitudinal validation of supermarket customer segments; it supports evaluating whether a segment persists across periods instead of treating a single clustering run as validation.
cards.limitations: The supermarket setting and private data are not equivalent to the current banking events or Tempo users.
cards.transferability_note: Use as a methodological prompt for repeated-period validation only.

cards.title: Monitoring customer-segment dynamics
cards.methodological_claim: The source addresses monitoring how customer segments change, supporting explicit monitoring of drift and reassignment when new behavioral observations arrive.
cards.limitations: The study uses online retail data and cannot validate the current segment sizes, product fit or audience demand.
cards.transferability_note: It supports a monitoring plan, not a claim that the current segments will remain stable.

cards.title: UK retail clustering algorithm comparison
cards.methodological_claim: The source compares clustering approaches in retail, supporting selection of algorithms by measurable structure, interpretability and business use rather than by algorithm popularity.
cards.limitations: The benchmark is a different retail population and does not contain the current banking event semantics.
cards.transferability_note: Transfer the comparison procedure, not any reported cluster labels, scores or customer value conclusions.

cards.title: Empirical comparison of RFM clustering approaches
cards.methodological_claim: The source is an empirical comparison of RFM clustering approaches; it supports treating RFM choices and algorithm comparison as methodological decisions that require validation.
cards.limitations: The empirical company data and commercial context are not available for the current audience decision.
cards.transferability_note: Do not use reported scores or customer-value labels as forecasts for this product or segment set.
